topics.title: Preoperative assessment: the map
lines: Before the first incision, thirteen topics decide whether and how we operate.
Three happen at the bedside: the cardiovascular history, the systems enquiry, and the examination.

Nine are investigations: routine laboratory tests, the chest radiograph, computed tomography, cardiac catheterization, coronary imaging, hemodynamics, echocardiography, echo interpretation, and perfusion and viability.
The last is the general pre-op checklist.
The cardiovascular history has three aims: establish the indications for surgery, identify issues that need management outside standard protocols, and define the preoperative estimate of risk.
The systems enquiry looks for problems that alter standard management, contraindications to elective surgery, and problems that could delay discharge.
The examination finds disease that needs investigating, helps plan the surgery, and spots problems that may delay recovery.
So ask every time: why operate, what must change, and what could go wrong.
topics.takeaway: Thirteen topics decide whether and how we operate: history, systems and examination first, then nine investigations and the checklist.

topics.title: Angina is not always chest pain
lines: Angina is not always a crushing chest pain.
The textbook picture is central, crushing pain, spreading to the jaw and down the left arm.
But patients may describe heaviness, indigestion, pain only in the arm, neck or jaw, nausea, or just fatigue.
So ask what brings it on: exertion, stress, emotion, and cold air.
And what relieves it: rest, or sublingual nitroglycerine.
Then count the spray: how many times a day do they need it?
Finally, grade it. The Canadian Cardiovascular Society scale applies to angina only.
Class one: no angina with ordinary activity. Class two: slight limitation.
Class three: marked limitation. Class four: angina on minimal exertion, or at rest.
Classes three and four carry increased risk.
Describe it, trigger it, relieve it, count it, grade it.
topics.takeaway: Describe it, trigger it, relieve it, count it, grade it.

topics.title: How breathless is the patient?
lines: How breathless is the patient, and why?
Start with exertional dyspnea and classify it on the New York Heart Association scale.
Class one: no limitation during ordinary activity. Class two: slight limitation.
Class three: marked limitation. Class four: no physical activity without symptoms.
Heart failure is defined as class three or four.
The same scale also grades angina.
Then look for other precipitants: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations.

lines.text: Chest infections, COPD, pulmonary embolism, and drugs such as β-blockers can all contribute.
lines.say: Chest infections, C O P D, pulmonary embolism, and drugs such as beta-blockers can all contribute.

lines: Ask about associated symptoms: peripheral edema, palpitations, wheeze, and sputum.

lines.text: And what helps: NTG, rest, or sitting up.
lines.say: And what helps: nitroglycerine, rest, or sitting up.

lines: Classify it. Define failure at class three. Then hunt for the cause.
topics.takeaway: Classify it. Define failure at class three. Then hunt for the cause.

topics.title: When was the last heart attack?
lines: When was the last heart attack?
For every previous infarction, document the number, the dates, and the coronary anatomy.

lines.text: Check the chart, and look for Q waves on the EKG.
lines.say: Check the chart, and look for Q waves on the E K G.

lines.text: Surgical risk is higher after a recent STEMI than after an NSTEMI.
lines.say: Surgical risk is higher after a recent stemmy than after an en stemmy.

lines: And it is highest early after the infarct, falling after one week.
Now previous stents and angioplasty. Note the left ventricular function and coronary anatomy from the angiography report.
Record how many procedures, when, what type, and the result.

lines.text: Emergency surgery after a failed PCI is high risk.
lines.say: Emergency surgery after a failed P C I is high risk.

lines.text: And after a recent PCI, clopidogrel usually continues for at least one month, which can change how bypass is done.
lines.say: And after a recent P C I, clopidogrel usually continues for at least one month, which can change how bypass is done.

lines: Count, date, anatomy, timing. Then the stent story.
topics.takeaway: Count, date, anatomy, timing. Then the stent story.
topics.note: Book p 2 prints 'non-ST segment elevation MI (STEMI)'; the second term is a typo for NSTEMI and is narrated as NSTEMI.

topics.title: A previous operation changes the next one
lines: A previous operation changes the next one.
Find it three ways: ask, check the chart, and look.
Look carefully at the whole chest, and the back, for scars.
A scar is the quickest clue when the history is vague.
Previous cardiac surgery adds to operative mortality, and needs several changes to the standard approach.
That added risk is incremental, on top of every other factor.

lines.text: That is why most patients should have a CT of the chest.
lines.say: That is why most patients should have a C T of the chest.

lines: It shows how the aorta and the right ventricle sit behind the sternum.
And where the patent bypass grafts run.
Those relationships decide how safely the chest can be reopened.
The scan needs intravenous contrast.
And always obtain the operative report: it records what was done.

lines.text: Scars. CT. Contrast. Report.
lines.say: Scars. C T. Contrast. Report.

topics.note: Sentences 'why2' and 'report' give the purpose of the scan and report; the book states the items, not the purpose.

topics.title: A black-out is not always the heart
lines: A black-out is not always the heart.

lines.text: Think epilepsy, TIAs, low blood sugar, or a vasovagal faint.
lines.say: Think epilepsy, T I As, low blood sugar, or a vasovagal faint.

lines: Vasovagal faints follow standing, emotion, coughing, or passing urine.
True cardiac syncope from aortic stenosis is usually exertional.
If it happens sitting or lying, think arrhythmia.
Dizziness is different: it can come before a faint, but it is fairly non-specific.
Common culprits are drugs: antianginals, antihypertensives, and diuretics, causing postural hypotension.
It can also reflect low cardiac output, from failure, arrhythmia or ischemia, or cerebrovascular disease.
And do not forget diabetic autonomic neuropathy: probably under-recognized.
When did it happen? What were they doing? What are they taking?
topics.takeaway: When did it happen? What were they doing? What are they taking?

topics.title: What does a palpitation feel like?
lines: What does a palpitation actually feel like?
To the patient it may be skipped beats, a racing heart, an irregular rhythm, or simply awareness of the heartbeat, especially at night.
Then ask about onset and offset.
Rapid onset and offset suggests a paroxysmal arrhythmia: it switches on and off.
Gradual onset and offset suggests sinus tachycardia: it fades in and out.
Preoperative atrial fibrillation may need ablation, left atrial appendage ligation, and warfarin.
Now swelling. Peripheral edema can follow changes in diuretic therapy, weight gain, or worse breathlessness.
It helps quantify the heart failure.
Ask what it felt like, how it started and stopped, and whether the ankles swell.
topics.takeaway: Ask what it felt like, how it started and stopped, and whether the ankles swell.

topics.title: Arteries elsewhere change the operation
lines: Arteries elsewhere change the operation here.

lines.text: Ask specifically about TIAs, strokes, claudication, and vascular interventions.
lines.say: Ask specifically about T I As, strokes, claudication, and vascular interventions.

lines.text: A history of TIAs warrants a carotid duplex to exclude carotid disease.
lines.say: A history of T I As warrants a carotid duplex to exclude carotid disease.

lines: Because arteriopathy outside the heart feeds the risk score, changes the stroke and limb-ischemia risk you quote at consent, and influences the conduit and cannulation site.
Then the risk factors. Some can be fixed in hospital: smoking, cholesterol, obesity, hypertension and diabetes.
Some cannot: male sex, age, and family history.

lines.text: Be precise. Non-smoker is not the same as smoked 60 a day and stopped two weeks ago.
lines.say: Be precise. Non-smoker is not the same as smoked sixty a day and stopped two weeks ago.

lines: Check the carotids. Fix what can be fixed. Be exact.
topics.takeaway: Check the carotids. Fix what can be fixed. Be exact.

topics.title: Valve patients have their own checklist
lines: Valve patients have their own checklist.
Note the type and degree of valve disease, and the left ventricular function from the echo.
Those facts shape both the operation and the risk.
Ask about rheumatic disease and endocarditis.
Both can damage valves, and both change the plan.
Make sure a dentist has recently cleared the mouth. Patients with no teeth do not need one.
Check there is no active source of infection, because infection threatens a new valve.

lines.text: Check they have had an angiogram if they are men over 45, postmenopausal women, have angina-type symptoms, or multiple coronary risk factors.
lines.say: Check they have had an angiogram if they are men over forty-five, postmenopausal women, have angina-type symptoms, or multiple coronary risk factors.

lines: And confirm the type of valve replacement has been discussed.
Valve, history, teeth, infection, angiogram, choice.
topics.takeaway: Valve, history, teeth, infection, angiogram, choice.
topics.note: 'which would threaten a new valve' is the reason for the infection check; the book lists the check without the reason.

topics.title: Ask the question twice
lines: Ask the question twice.
Any other medical problems? Ever in hospital for anything other than the heart? Any operations, ever?
Be persistent: patients often forget important chronic illnesses and operations.

lines.text: Previous chest radiotherapy means a CT scan, because the aorta may be calcified.
lines.say: Previous chest radiotherapy means a C T scan, because the aorta may be calcified.

lines: Malignant disease needs careful evaluation: in most cases, metastatic spread is a relative contraindication to cardiac surgery.
Thyroid disease may dictate the choice of antiarrhythmic.
A hip replacement means a pillow between the legs when transferring, because adducting the hip can dislocate it.
Blood dyscrasias, thrombocytopenia, factor deficiencies, thrombophilias, need a hematologist.
And diabetes has its own pre-op plan.
Every flag has an action.

topics.title: Every drug has a clock
lines: Every drug has a clock.

lines.text: Antianginals and β-blockers continue until surgery.
lines.say: Antianginals and beta-blockers continue until surgery.

lines.text: Afterwards, antianginals stop; β-blockers return as pressure and rhythm allow.
lines.say: Afterwards, antianginals stop; beta-blockers return as pressure and rhythm allow.

lines.text: ACE inhibitors stop 24–48 hours before, to avoid profound peripheral dilatation afterwards.
lines.say: ace inhibitors stop twenty-four to forty-eight hours before, to avoid profound peripheral dilatation afterwards.

lines.text: Aspirin and clopidogrel: many surgeons stop them 5–10 days before, because they increase bleeding.
lines.say: Aspirin and clopidogrel: many surgeons stop them five to ten days before, because they increase bleeding.

lines.text: But ischemic risk rises slightly, so high-risk patients, such as recent PCI or a tight left main, may continue.
lines.say: But ischemic risk rises slightly, so high-risk patients, such as recent P C I or a tight left main, may continue.

lines: Warfarin stops five days before. If thromboembolic risk is high, admit early for intravenous heparin.
Steroids: above five milligrams of prednisone daily, give hydrocortisone cover from the premedication, to avoid an Addisonian crisis.
Long-acting hypoglycemics are withheld on the morning of surgery, with an insulin sliding scale if needed.
Continue, stop, or decide: know the clock for each.
topics.takeaway: Continue, stop, or decide: know the clock for each.

topics.title: Allergies that change the operation
lines: Allergies: the ones that change the operation.
Take every drug, dose and regimen, and every allergy: drugs, iodine, contrast, and fish.
Fish matters because protamine is made from salmon sperm.
On bypass, the blood is anticoagulated with heparin, and protamine reverses it at the end.
Latex allergy means changing the equipment, so warn the operating room.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is the opposite problem: heparin itself is the culprit.
Those patients may need a heparin-free bypass with bivalirudin or argatroban, which mandates careful pre-planning.
Iodine and contrast allergies matter for every scan and angiogram that follows.
Fish, latex, heparin, contrast: four allergies, four plans.
topics.takeaway: Fish, latex, heparin, contrast: four allergies, four plans.
topics.note: 'On bypass ... protamine reverses it' and 'every scan and angiogram that follows' are supporting explanations from standard practice; the book page lists the allergies only.

topics.title: Social history is part of the surgical plan
lines: Social history is part of the surgical plan.
Jehovah's Witness patients do not accept blood or blood products, and some refuse cell salvage.
Identify them early, counsel them, document their preferences, and aim for a hematocrit above forty percent.
Several weeks of erythropoietin may be indicated.
Heavy or binge drinkers risk alcohol withdrawal.

lines.text: Avoid haloperidol: it lowers the seizure threshold and prolongs the QT interval.
lines.say: Avoid haloperidol: it lowers the seizure threshold and prolongs the Q T interval.

lines: Prescribe diazepam, two milligrams orally every eight hours, with thiamine and folate.
If the patient lives alone, plan rehabilitation.
If they use a stick or frame, involve physiotherapists early, because sternal union may be compromised even if mobility is not.

lines.text: And ask about TIAs, strokes and residual deficit, and identify dementia: advanced dementia is a contraindication to cardiac surgery.
lines.say: And ask about T I As, strokes and residual deficit, and identify dementia: advanced dementia is a contraindication to cardiac surgery.

lines: Blood, alcohol, home, brain.

topics.title: A cold can cancel the operation
lines: A cold can cancel the operation.
An active upper respiratory tract infection is sufficient reason to cancel, so ask about cough, colds and sputum.

lines.text: If you suspect one, measure the temperature, C-reactive protein and white cell count, and get a chest X-ray.
lines.say: If you suspect one, measure the temperature, C reactive protein and white cell count, and get a chest X-ray.

lines.text: Assess COPD by asking about admissions, inhalers, nebulizers and home oxygen.
lines.say: Assess C O P D by asking about admissions, inhalers, nebulizers and home oxygen.

lines: If breathlessness dominates, get lung function tests, including blood gases.
Now the gut. Cardiac surgery carries a risk of upper G I bleeding from peptic ulcers, prolonged ileus, and flares of pancreatitis or cholecystitis.
So ask about dyspepsia, ulcers and pancreatitis.
Start every patient on a proton pump inhibitor.

lines.text: Flag the drug chart: no NSAIDs in at-risk patients, and give aspirin enteric-coated, with food.
lines.say: Flag the drug chart: no en seds in at-risk patients, and give aspirin enteric-coated, with food.

lines.text: Lungs: infection and COPD. Gut: ask, protect, avoid NSAIDs.
lines.say: Lungs: infection and C O P D. Gut: ask, protect, avoid en seds.

topics.takeaway: Lungs: infection and COPD. Gut: ask, protect, avoid NSAIDs.

topics.title: The kidneys can delay the operation
lines: The kidneys can delay the operation.
Check the notes for renal dysfunction.
If there is an acute deterioration, it may be worth delaying surgery to optimize.

lines.text: Stop nephrotoxic drugs, including ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs, start intravenous fluids with careful balance, and sometimes dialyze.
lines.say: Stop nephrotoxic drugs, including ace inhibitors and en seds, start intravenous fluids with careful balance, and sometimes dialyze.

lines: Dialysis patients should be dialyzed the morning of surgery, or the night before.
Cardiac catheterization adds its own risk.
Fasting leaves the patient hypovolemic, and the contrast is nephrotoxic.
So prescribe intravenous fluid if renal function is borderline, and consider intravenous acetylcysteine before contrast studies.
And if the history suggests prostatic enlargement, warn the patient they may need a suprapubic catheter.
Protect, hydrate, dialyze, warn.

topics.title: The short examination
lines: Eight steps make the short examination.
Its purposes: find disease that needs investigating, help plan the surgery, and spot problems that may delay recovery.
For the average elective patient, a shortened version is sufficient.
One: pulse, rate and rhythm. Two: blood pressure.

lines.text: Three: jugular venous pressure, with the patient at 45°.
lines.say: Three: jugular venous pressure, with the patient at forty-five degrees.

lines: Four: auscultate the heart sounds, the carotids, and the breath sounds, and look for scars.
Five: the abdomen: tenderness, hernias, organomegaly, scars.
Six: feel the peripheral pulses, including the abdominal aorta.
Seven: assess pedal edema. Eight: assess the conduits, the vessels that may become grafts.
Pulse, pressure, veins, chest, abdomen, pulses, edema, conduits.
topics.takeaway: Pulse, pressure, veins, chest, abdomen, pulses, edema, conduits.
topics.note: 'the vessels that may become grafts' explains 'conduits' (standard meaning in bypass surgery).

topics.title: Examine from the end of the bed
lines: Examine from the end of the bed.
Is the patient comfortable at rest, or requiring oxygen? Well, or moribund? Obese, or cachectic?
Look for features of Down's syndrome, which suggests an atrial or ventricular septal defect, and Marfan syndrome, which suggests aortic aneurysm, dissection and incompetence.

lines.text: Then position the patient at 45°.
lines.say: Then position the patient at forty-five degrees.

lines: Now the hands and forearms. Nicotine staining.
And the stigmata of endocarditis: splinter hemorrhages.
Osler's nodes: tender lumps in the fingertip pulps.
Janeway lesions: red macules on the palms or the flexor aspects of the wrists.
Tendon xanthomas. And petechiae, which may be present in infective endocarditis.
Bed-end, syndromes, hands: what the surface says about valves and aorta.
topics.takeaway: Bed-end, syndromes, hands: what the surface says about valves and aorta.

topics.title: Pulse, pressure and face
lines: Pulse, pressure and face each point to a diagnosis.
Rate and rhythm at the radial pulse. Character and volume at the brachial or carotid.
Aortic stenosis classically gives a slow-rising, thready pulse.
Aortic incompetence gives a large-volume bounding pulse.

lines.text: Blood pressure: a systolic above 180 should be treated with nifedipine, ten milligrams sublingually, before surgery.
lines.say: Blood pressure: a systolic above one hundred and eighty should be treated with nifedipine, ten milligrams sublingually, before surgery.

lines: A wide pulse pressure suggests aortic incompetence.
Use a broad cuff for large arms, or the pressure is underestimated.
Check both arms if you suspect aortic dissection or coarctation.
The face: a malar flush, cyanosis in a butterfly distribution, is characteristic of mitral stenosis.
In the eyes: jaundice from hemolysis with prosthetic valves, xanthelasma and corneal arcus with hyperlipidemia, and Roth spots in endocarditis.
Slow pulse, wide pressure, malar flush: three signs, three valves.
topics.takeaway: Slow pulse, wide pressure, malar flush: three signs, three valves.
